items.title: Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay Wins the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
items.standfirst: The South African jurist has been recognized “for her efforts to promote peace and international law,” said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.
items.content: Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, a South African jurist and former U.N. high commissioner for human rights, won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize on Friday “for her efforts to promote peace and international law.” “Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career. Born into a family of Indian Tamil origin under apartheid in Durban, South Africa, Pillay became a lawyer and legal pioneer, confronting deep structural discrimination, segregation, and exclusion,” said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, a South African jurist and former U.N. high commissioner for human rights, won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize on Friday “for her efforts to promote peace and international law.”“Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career. Born into a family of Indian Tamil origin under apartheid in Durban, South Africa, Pillay became a lawyer and legal pioneer, confronting deep structural discrimination, segregation, and exclusion,” said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee. “A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time.”Pillay, 85, is a judge on the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in the case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide. She was also chair of the ⁠U.N. Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory that concluded last year that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. (Israel at the time dismissed the report as "scandalous" and “fake.") Israel's Foreign Ministry criticized Pillay's win, referring to it as a "grotesque weaponization" of the award.In "historic international court cases, she has shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence," Frydnes said, referring to Pillay as "one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time."Reflecting on her win, Pillay said she is often asked when she will stop working. "I can’t obviously stop my work in support of the Nuremberg Principles, because of the people we meet here," she said.Pillay's career spans more than 50 yearsBorn in South Africa in 1941, Pillay was the first non-white woman to establish a legal practice in the country, according to the U.N.In those early years of practicing law, she acted as a defense attorney for anti-apartheid activists.Pillay has served as a judge on the High Court in South Africa, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, and the International Criminal Court (ICC) throughout the course of her career.She was the U.N. human rights chief from September 2008 to August 2014. Volker Türk, who currently holds that position, said Pillay's Nobel recognition is "particularly poignant" as it comes "at a time when human rights are under attack on so many fronts, including from those who wield enormous power."“It is an award to all those who around the world dedicate their lives to the defense of human rights, often at great risk to their security," he added.Pillay is the fifth South African national to be awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. She follows in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela, FW de Klerk, Archbishop Desmond ​Tutu, and Albert Luthuli.Pillay dedicates award to "survivors of international crimes"Pillay dedicated her Nobel Peace Prize to “all of the survivors of international crimes” and people defending international criminal justice, “whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign.”During a press conference at the International Nuremberg Principle Academy, in the German city where the trials of Nazi leaders showcased the enforcement of international law, Pillay referred to the award as a "wonderful surprise" and the "highest honor."Using her platform to spotlight the international justice system, Pillay told reporters: “We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack... This worsening reality is particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court."She added that the Nobel recognition has strengthened her "conviction that we must stand together in ‌defense of the rule of law, ​in defense of independent courts, and an international legal order ⁠based on principle."Trump Admin announces sanctions against the ICC hours after winWhen asked during a press briefing if the award sends a message to those who question or sanction international courts, Frydnes told reporters: “This is definitely a message to those who are attacking, undermin[ing] the international system, the international rules-based system, and the institutions."U.S. President Donald Trump last month called for countries to "immediately" resign from the International Criminal Court (ICC), amid a broader push by the Trump Administration to dismantle the institution it accuses of unfairly targeting the U.S. and Israel. His call was firmly rejected by European leaders.The Trump Administration has criticized the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli leaders, including ​Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and former investigations into the actions of American soldiers in Afghanistan.Hours after Pillay's win, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the Trump Administration is placing sweeping new sanctions on the ICC. It has previously imposed sanctions on the court's prosecutors and judges, but these new measures go a step further.“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us,” Rubio said. “The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC.”As a result of the sanctions, and "subject to applicable licenses and exceptions, all property and interests in property of the ICC that are in the United States or in possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control," read a notice from the State Department.Rubio claimed both Republicans and Democrats have concerns about the court overstepping its jurisdiction, but said only Trump is willing to take action. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC," he warned.In response, the ICC's deputy ​prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan condemned the sanctions and vowed the court's "work will ​continue ⁠across all our situations, our ⁠investigations, ​and our ​prosecution."The Foreign Ministers of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, and the U.K. have also denounced the sanctions.In a joint statement that expressed "unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC," the officials said the sanctions "will have a significant impact on the [ICC's] work, its dedicated staff, and their families."Pillay pokes fun at Trump as she reacts to awardPillay referenced Trump and his well-documented campaign to be awarded the Nobel Peace Prize when she reacted to her own recognition on Friday morning. In a video shared by Agnes Callamard, secretary general of Amnesty International, Pillay could be seen entering a room at Nuremberg Court to resounding applause from her peers. "If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump," she joked.The 2025 Nobel Peace Prize winner, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, famously gave her medal to Trump in January as she pressed the U.S. to support democracy in Venezuela.While the Norwegian Nobel Institute doesn’t release a shortlist of its contenders each year, the leaders of Israel, Cambodia, and Pakistan have all previously said they nominated Trump. The institute registered a total of 287 candidates for this year’s prize, including 208 individuals and 79 organizations.Trump said earlier this week it would be a “great discredit” to the Norwegian Nobel Committee if they did not announce him as this year's recipient.

items.title: Trump Taps Katie Zacharia to Replace Karoline Leavitt as White House Press Secretary
items.standfirst: Zacharia, a conservative commentator, will succeed Karoline Leavitt in the position.
items.content: —Terry Wyatt—Getty Images for 2521 Entertainment and Angel StudiosPresident Donald Trump has selected conservative commentator Katie Zacharia to serve as the next White House press secretary, he announced Friday.Zacharia will replace Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down in August, in the position. Zacharia currently works as a communications adviser at Trump Media and Technology Group, the company that runs Trump’s social media platform Truth Social. She previously worked at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) as a spokesperson for former Secretary Kristi Noem, and appears frequently on conservative media including Fox News and Newsmax. In a post on Truth Social announcing his selection, Trump praised Zacharia for “an unblemished record of support” and being “a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning.” “She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!” Trump continued. “I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration.”The New York Times first reported that Zacharia had been tapped by the White House. Zacharia, who currently lives in California and graduated from Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, has also worked as a general counsel for almost three years at Fix California, a conservative non-profit founded by Ric Grenell, who served as Acting Director of National Intelligence during Trump’s first Administration. The organization works to promote a conservative agenda around the state.In June, Zacharia was appointed to the advisory board of NovaRed Mining Inc, a Canadian mining company based in Vancouver, according to a company announcement. Just a week before Zacharia’s appointment, Noem also joined the advisory board.Leavitt, who became the youngest White House press secretary in history at the age of 27, this week joined Fox News as an on-air contributor, the network announced on Monday. She is the third of Trump’s former press secretaries to join the network. She begins on Nov. 1.Trump announced Leavitt’s departure through a Truth Social post in which he said that she “will now be one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party, as we work to defy History, and conclusively win the Midterm Elections.”Leavitt responded with a lengthy post on X in which she thanked the President and the White House and said that she would remain “a vocal advocate for MAGA and the Republican Party. ”Leavitt gave birth to her second child, Viviana, in May. She went on maternity leave that month and later announced that she would be stepping down from her role to spend more time with her family. Trump’s time in office has been characterized by a contentious relationship with the media, which he has repeatedly attacked and derided while serving as President. Leavitt echoed that attitude during her time behind the podium, becoming known for her acerbic remarks and quick deflections during press briefings.Zacharia will enter the White House during a fight over the media’s access to the President. Trump on Sept. 18 banned POLITICO, CNN, and MS NOW from the White House grounds, sparking an ongoing legal battle. Though the outlets’ access to the White House has been restored after a federal judge issued a temporary restraining order against the ban, Trump has since restricted POLITICO and CNN from boarding Air Force One, preventing them from carrying out their White House pool duties and drawing further blowback. Zacharia would also be entering the White House at a time when Trump is facing record-low approval ratings over his handling of the war in Iran, which has contributed to rising inflation in the U.S., and as the fast-approaching November midterms threaten Republicans’ control over both chambers of Congress.

items.title: Trump establishes committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa Cook
items.standfirst: US president renews his efforts to oust Cook despite supreme court ruling that her firing was unconstitutionalDonald Trump announced on Friday that he is establishing a committee to investigate Lisa Cook, the US Federal Reserve governor, over allegations that she committed mortgage fraud, renewing his efforts to oust her despite a June supreme court ruling that her earlier firing was unconstitutional.Trump said a committee will consult with justice department officials to decide whether there is “cause” for her removal. The White House will hold an in-person hearing on 5 November to consider the allegations against Cook, which will be closed to the public but transcribed and published. Cook will be able to submit a written statement to present her own evidence and will be subject to examination from White House and her own legal counsel. Continue reading...

items.standfirst: The response to the incident tests the friendship between the New York mayor and the President.
items.content: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks during a press conference at the site where a man was shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer during an operation in the Bronx, on Oct. 8, 2026. —Ryan Murphy—Getty ImagesNew York Mayor Zohran Mamdani wants President Donald Trump to put an end to Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s operations in the city after an agent-involved shooting injured one person on Thursday.“This is an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation,” Mamdani said in a statement Thursday evening. “I have called the President; when we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city. I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities.”New York police said that around 4 p.m., federal agents got involved in a shooting and injured a man in the city’s Marble Hill residential section. The police’s afternoon statement said the shooting victim was conscious and receiving medical attention in a nearby hospital.But at a press conference Thursday evening before furious protesters, Mamdani said that after his two-hour conversation with Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, he has failed to negotiate the release of the shooting victim.The response to the shooting tests Mamdani’s charm offensive with the President, who appears unlikely to budge on his immigration agenda despite previous friendliness with the Democratic mayor. Despite wide ideological differences, Trump and Mamdani have had a cordial relationship.Mamdani, however, remains just as firm on his own side of the issue. A steadfast critic of ICE operations, he has backed calls to abolish the agency. “I have said this directly—whether to the President or to the public—ICE undermines public safety,” he said.The White House pointed TIME to the Department of Homeland Security’s statement, which attacked New York’s “sanctuary politicians” that limit cooperation with federal agents. Homeland Security Secretary Markewayne Mullin responded directly to Mamdani at a press conference Friday morning, accusing the mayor of “inciting hostilities" and undermining ICE's mission. Mullin said he had spoken with Mamdani multiple times on Thursday night. Besides Mamdani, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, also a Democrat, released a swift rebuke of the shooting and said she too spoke with Trump and Mullin. “New Yorkers have witnessed far too many acts of violence by a rogue federal agency and untrained agents that operate with impunity,” the governor said. “Federal authorities need to provide answers, and they must do so immediately.”What happened?City police commissioner Jessica Tisch said that based on initial information, police received multiple 911 calls around 4 p.m. reporting shots fired and a person shot near 2 Marble Hill Avenue. Protesters gather near the scene where a man was shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer during an operation in the Bronx borough of New York on October 8, 2026. —Charly Triballeau—AFP/Getty ImagesTheir preliminary investigation showed that federal immigration agents were “conducting a targeted enforcement operation” to take a person in a gray vehicle into custody. Their target, whom Tisch identified as 28-year-old Oscar Belgal, was with a 5-year-old boy, whom police believed to be his son. Tisch said that one plainclothes federal agent approached the driver’s side window, with his gun drawn, with another plainclothes agent near the headlight, before the vehicle moved forward. According to evidence collected on the scene, Tisch said that at least one ICE agent fired seven rounds, “striking the driver in the neck below his left ear.”DHS said in its statement that an ICE officer “discharged his weapon” and injured its target, whom ICE agents immediately rendered aid to. “The incident remains under investigation,” the department added.Tisch added that when New York police arrived on scene, they saw men in various clothes, including “at least one carrying a long gun.” Police also saw the injured Belgal “handcuffed and seated on the ground,” and they “immediately” placed him into a police vehicle and gave aid, before transporting him to New York-Presbyterian Allen Hospital in stable condition. The child, meanwhile, is safe and in the care of a family member, Tisch added. Mullin said Friday that the ICE officers involved in the shooting were wearing body cameras and that there was footage relating to the incident. “As the investigation moves forward, as I said, we’ll release the information,” he said.What do we know about the victim?Tisch said that Belgal had two prior arrests in New York City: “one for robbery in 2023 in which he pleaded guilty to fourth-degree grand larceny and received five years probation; and one for criminal sale of a controlled substance in 2025, which is still pending.” DHS did not name Belgal, but it described the target of the ICE operation as a “criminal illegal” immigrant from the Dominican Republic “with a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession.”The department alleged the shooting victim had ties to the Trinitarios gang, which was involved in the shooting of an off-duty Customs and Border Protection officer last year. It added that police arrested the target on Dec. 7, 2023, “but was released into the community a few days later by reckless Democrat sanctuary policies that put American lives at risk.” Mullin said Friday morning that Bengal was "affiliated with a gang" and that ICE believed Bengal had knowledge regarding the shooting of a CBP officer last year. He also said ICE had attempted, and failed, to detain Bengal in September.What have been the reactions?The New York City shooting is just the latest in a spate of violent incidents involving federal immigration agents. Tallies from the New York Times and ABC News show more than 20 people shot, with at least six killed, including three U.S. citizens: Renee Good, Alex Pretti, and Ruben Ray Martinez. Read More: These Two Brothers Are Fighting to Protect Immigrant Families After a TragedyThe city has also become a hotspot for ICE-related activity. As Gothamist reported on Oct. 7, more than 8,800—or nearly half—of all ICE arrests in New York state during the second-term Trump Administration have happened in New York City’s five boroughs.Lawmakers have since debated the nationwide enforcement of Trump’s immigration agenda, leading to funding battles and partial shutdowns of DHS.Mamdani and other New York politicians took issue with how the ICE operation could have endangered a child. “There is no explanation for federal officers firing this many rounds into a car that has a 5-year-old,” the New York mayor said in the press conference.Rep. Ritchie Torres, who represents the Bronx, posted that “firing multiple rounds into a car with a child inside, on a busy residential street in the Bronx, is abhorrent and indefensible.”Rep. Adriano Espaillat, the Democrat representing the district covering Upper Manhattan and parts of West Bronx, posted on social media that ICE has denied him as well as the victim’s family from visiting and checking on the victim. Espaillat said he met the victim’s 5-year-old son, “distraught and traumatized after witnessing this horrific event.”Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who represents New York and led the legislative standoff that temporarily blocked funding for DHS, called the shooting “deeply disturbing, especially amid reports that a child was in the car when shots were fired.” The senator called on DHS to release body camera footage and ensure independent investigations.—With reporting by Philip Wang

items.title: Nicolás Maduro and his wife indicted for alleged torture of US citizens
items.standfirst: Ousted Venezuelan president and Cilia Flores have been in jail in New York since early JanuaryThe deposed Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been indicted for alleged conspiracy to commit torture, according to Manhattan federal court papers unsealed on Thursday.The superseding indictment was unsealed shortly before Flores appeared at court in her ongoing push for pretrial release – which was denied by Judge Alvin Hellerstein. Maduro and Flores have been jailed in New York City since early January. Continue reading...
